extracted.intended_audience: Lawyers, government contracting officers, claimants, and others advising or litigating about U.S. federal government contracts (esp. under §3744 R.S.)
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and standards governing when contracts with the United States must be in writing and signed, the legal effect of informal/oral agreements or partial performance, statutory/regulatory exceptions, and remedies (implied recovery, set-off, supplemental agreements).

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing and signature requirement (section 3744, R.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: It makes it unlawful for contracting officers to make contracts in any other way than by writing signed by the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statute is mandatory where it applies; contracts required by the statute must be reduced to writing and signed with the parties' names at the end. Rationale: prevent frauds and perjuries and restrain officers from making reckless engagements. If not complied with, the agreement is void as a contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary memoranda, bids, and letter acceptances are not contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters of offer and acceptance, or other preliminary memoranda made in preparing a contract for execution in the form required by law, do not constitute a contract within the meaning of section 3744, R.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance by letter or correspondence that does not produce a written signed contract is typically 'preliminary' only; either party may legally refuse to carry out the bid. (Cases: South Boston Iron Co. v. U.S., International Contracting Co. v. Lamont, and others.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Part performance of void informal contract — implied recovery for fair value
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract void because not in writing has been wholly or partially executed, the party so performing will be entitled to recover the fair value of the property or services furnished as upon an implied contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts award reasonable value for work/materials actually furnished even if the agreement was void for lack of writing. Example: owner of vessel whose unwritten agreement with government was void recovered only fair use value ($1,200) rather than agreed $60,000.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full performance may permit recovery of agreed price despite void instrument (St. Louis Hay & Grain rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: After actual performance, on the strength of the agreement, recovery may be had for the amount agreed upon, notwithstanding the instrument itself was void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the informal agreement was fully executed and the Government accepted/paid under its terms, the party cannot later claim more than the price agreed upon; a lawful transfer executed pursuant to the agreement fixes the parties' obligations (St. Louis Hay & Grain Co. v. U.S.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Parol evidence rule against adding terms to an unambiguous written contract
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contract is not ambiguous or technically obscure, parol evidence is not admissible to establish a new term or add an understanding at variance with its written stipulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the written contract expresses the final agreement, prior oral understandings (e.g., about deductions or additional obligations) cannot be enforced against the United States. Example: claimed oral agreement to permit deductions was estopped.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions for exigency or emergency (immediate delivery/performance)
rubrics_metrics.description: If there is an exigency or emergency requiring immediate delivery of property or immediate rendition of services a written contract is not necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emergency contracts (including wartime exigencies) are recognized as exceptions to the writing requirement. Cases and regulations (par. 558 A.R. 1910, Ceballos v. U.S.) allow oral or other expedited methods when immediate performance follows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time extensions: oral waiver vs. specific-date extension
rubrics_metrics.description: The time fixed in an existing written contract for completion may be orally waived (extended indefinitely), and the written contract will continue in force with a reasonable time for performance; but if it is desired to extend the time to a specific date, section 3744 applies and the extension should be by formal written contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefinite or reasonable extensions by oral agreement are permissible; however, creating a binding, specific new deadline requires compliance with the writing/signature statute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army Regulations — three procurement methods and their effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph 549, Army Regulations (558 of 1910) provides three methods: (1) by contract reduced to writing and signed; (2) by written proposal and written acceptance; (3) by oral agreement. The first method constitutes a 'contract' under section 3744, but the second does not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The regulation permits method (2) only when delivery or performance immediately follows the award; the regulation allows method (3) (oral) under limited circumstances (par. 559) only when delivery/performance immediately follows the agreement. Reason: binding future obligations require a written contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and regulatory exceptions to the writing requirement (specific acts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific statutes modify or except the application of section 3744 in certain contexts (e.g., Mar. 23, 1910 Ordnance act for certain Ordnance contracts, June 25, 1910 lease/hire exception for <=3 months, June 12, 1906 open market purchases up to $500, and special appropriations discretionary by the President).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These statutory provisions create narrow exceptions (by dollar amount, duration, subject matter, or discretion) where formal written contracts are not required; practitioners must check the precise statutory/regulatory language and thresholds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informal contract fully executed and accepted may be binding
rubrics_metrics.description: When an informal contract by proposal and acceptance has been fully executed on the part of the contractor and has been accepted by the Government, it becomes as binding as a formal contract, although not reduced to writing and signed, in some decisions (comptroller's holdings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Administrative decisions (e.g., XV Comp. Dec. 89) have held that a fully executed informal contract accepted by the Government can be treated as binding; filing proposals/acceptances with auditors may be required for audit purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parol increase/enlargement of written contract not binding; recovery for actual work possible
rubrics_metrics.description: A parol agreement enlarging the quantity of work required by a written contract is not obligatory upon the Government where the contract is required by law to be in writing; but compensation for work actually done may be recovered on an implied contract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Oral modifications that increase scope without formal supplemental contract are generally unenforceable against the Government, though the performer can recover reasonable value for additional work performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unsigned or contractor-signed-only extensions do not bind the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: A written agreement of extension signed only by the contractor was not a contract and gave the United States no rights in the premises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions or amendments must be signed by the proper government officer (and the contractor) with names at the end to be binding under section 3744; otherwise they may be ineffective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Renewal notices and short-form renewals must comply with signature requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A lease renewal by written notice with indorsement of acceptance by the lessor would not be binding unless signed by both parties 'with their names at the end thereof'; but a brief contract referring to the original lease, signed by the proper officer and the lessor with their names, would comply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical approach: to renew annually within the original term, prepare a short supplemental contract signed properly at each fiscal year beginning to meet statutory formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplemental agreements can be formed by certain signed correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contracting officer wrote terms desired for a supplemental agreement and the contractor returned the letter stating acceptance and signed it, with the surety's signed assent below, the paper constituted a written supplemental contract within the meaning of section 3744, R.S.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A contractor's signed acceptance on the officer's letter (with surety assent) can satisfy writing/signature formalities for a supplemental contract; placement and form of signatures matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuing proposals lacking consideration or officer signature are not binding contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'agreement' among carriers purporting to bind rates year-to-year but not signed by any officer of the United States and having no consideration is not a binding contract under section 3744, R.S., but simply a continuing proposal good until withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of authorized government signature and lack of consideration render such instruments non-binding; they remain offers until withdrawn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refusal to sign government form by an accepted bidder bars damages claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a bidder refused to sign the form of contract submitted to him after acceptance, and the Government entered into a contract with the next lowest bidder, the bidder who refused to sign had no legal claim for damages against the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptance followed by refusal to execute the required written contract typically defeats a claim for damages against the Government for lost opportunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grumbling consent by contractor does not defeat binding signed contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A contractor's 'grumbling consent' (signing under protest) to the terms insisted upon by the Government does not prevent the signed and approved contract from being the sole measure of rights and liabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the contractor signs and the proper authority approves, subsequent complaints or protests do not undo the binding effect of the executed contract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Death of contractor — payment to administrator; subcontractor's recourse
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contractor died prior to completion of work under a contract void because not in writing, and the work was completed by a subcontractor, payment of the reasonable value thereof should be made to the administrator of the estate of the decedent and the subcontractor must look to said estate for payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical consequence: liens by subcontractors do not displace the estate; claims flow through the contractor's estate when the primary contract obligations are with the contractor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set-off and withholding: liquidated vs. unliquidated claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In settling with a contractor under a duly executed contract, there may be set off against the amount due to him an amount due from him as damages under another contract if the amount due from him is a liquidated amount. Where the amount is not liquidated, the Government has no strict legal right to insist on set-off, but has an equitable right to withhold money until the unliquidated claim can be adjusted in the Court of Claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government practice permits withholding sums (even for unliquidated claims) sufficient to cover potential loss; parties may seek judicial adjustment. Examples show withholdings for uncertain losses pending Court of Claims resolution.
